text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London ended lower but roaster price- fixations at the lows and lack of fresh sales in the afternoon helped some positions to finish above the day's floor. July and September lost 80 cents to close at $1,825 and $1,850 per tonne respectively. Arabica futures in New York ended higher in dull trading in a technical correction to the market's recent sharp slide. July added 6.75 cents/lb to close at 237.25 cents/lb, while September ended 4.75 cents/lb higher at 214.15 cents/lb. The outer months gained between 0.75 to 4.15 cents/lb.

Market participants down-played news that the Brazilian government asked coffee exporters not to make any further sales for June shipment as under the ACPC retention scheme Brazil should not ship more than 6 million bags between January and June 1997. According to export statistics, shipments to the end of May had already exceeded this level.

There are several indications, that the tightness is not over yet and traders said there is very little tenderable coffee available for July and September and that certified coffee stocks are going to dwindle. This, it was added, suggests another period of rising prices. However, some pointed out that the pipeline held 3 to 5 million additional bags due to heavy shipments in the first half of 1997 and thus there is little reason for concern.

BRAZIL - Brazil's government has asked coffee exporters to make no further sales for June shipment after evaluating current exports in light of a limit agreed with other producing countries. The government also asked exporters to roll over as much as possible exports at the end of June until the beginning of July. Heavy rains in Brazil's coffee belt are interfering with harvesting, and quality could suffer as a result, trade sources said. Although the weather was ideal throughout May, the recent downpour in the coffee producing regions has led to much pessimism. Coffee harvested during heavy precipitation is more prone to damage and quality suffers as a result, it was added.

COLOMBIA - Coffee production during July/September is expected to total no more than 1.5 million 60-kg bags, well below average exports of 900,000 bags per month, the National Coffee Growers' Federation said. To help make up for the resulting shortfall and allow Colombia to export 2.5 million 60-kg bags during the three-month period, the federation plans to release up to 1 million bags of old crop coffee from its inventories for sale abroad, it was added. Trade sources in Colombia said that exports of 2.5 million bags for July/September might be too ambitious when one considers that production will be 1.5 million and some coffee will need to be used for domestic use and therefore the 1 million bags of old crop coffee might not be really available.
UNITED STATES - US certified coffee stocks are on the decline again. On June 5 stocks fell by 1,650 60-kg bags to 43,625 bags, down from 45,275 bags on June 5 and 45,702 bags on June 3.

AUSTRALIA - Australia imported 305,400 bags of coffee in January/April 1997, nearly 2 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1996. Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by 4 per cent to 845,200 bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/April 1997 were Vietnam (95,700 vs 96,500 bags) and Papua New Guinea (77,200 vs 82,400 bags).

TANZANIA - Tanzania exported 654,100 bags of coffee in July/April 1996/97 which compares to 741,400 bags exported the same period in 1995/96. Total exports in crop year 1995/96 (July/June) reached 921,000 bags, up from 612,000 bags the previous year. Main countries of destination in July/April 1996/97 were Germany (253,400 vs 252,300 bags) and Japan (103,800 vs 138,600 bags).
